column5: Aramaic dînâ, court, opened books
column6: The commentary's dīn as judgment and account meets Daniel's Aramaic dînâ: the court sits and books are opened, giving the cognate root a concrete eschatological reckoning scene.

column5: din ve-heshbon before the King of kings
column6: The commentary calls the day a judgment and account under its Mālik; Avot says each person will give din ve-heshbon, “judgment and account,” before the King of kings, using the Hebrew cognate in the same paired sense.

column5: shop, credit, open ledger, collectors
column6: Avot turns deferred credit into a moral accounting image: the shop gives credit, the ledger records it, and collectors exact payment. This closely supplies the commentary's debt, due date, record, and final recompense picture.

column5: king settling accounts with servants
column6: Jesus likens the kingdom to a king who begins to settle accounts with his servants; the king, reckoning, and unpaid obligation form a direct narrative counterpart to the commentary's ruler of the day of account.

column5: debt exacted under punishment
column6: In the same parable the master hands the debtor over until the whole debt is paid. It makes the commentary's due debt and punitive recompense a single judicial action.

column5: sealed deed, witnesses, weighed silver
column6: Jeremiah's land purchase is written and sealed, witnessed, and paid by weighing silver on scales. Its own legal transaction joins the commentary's written obligation, witnesses, price, and even balance imagery.

column5: God weighs hearts and repays deeds
column6: The proverb says the one who weighs hearts knows and repays each person according to work. It makes the commentary's unleaning balance explicitly a divine assessment followed by measured payment.

column5: a king weighed in balances
column6: Daniel tells Belshazzar that he has been weighed in the balances and found deficient. The judgment of a ruler through a balance directly realizes the commentary's kingly day and exact scale.

column5: just balance and weights belong to YHWH
column6: The commentary places a true balance within God's final reckoning; this proverb says the just balance, scales, and bag-weights are YHWH's work, grounding the image in divine rather than merely commercial justice.

column5: whole and just weight
column6: The command for a whole and just weight and measure gives a legal analogue to the commentary's full-weight coin that does not tip the scale.

column5: just scales, weights, ephah, and hin
column6: Leviticus requires just scales and measures in Israel's market. It supplies the ordinary ethical practice behind the commentary's image of an upright balance in the final account.

column5: acquittal and fraudulent scales
column6: Micah asks whether God can acquit someone with wicked scales and false weights. It explicitly fuses courtroom acquittal with commercial fraud, as the commentary fuses judgment day and a tilted balance.

column5: weighed in a just balance before God
column6: Job asks to be weighed in a just balance so that God may know his integrity. The balance is already a personal divine verdict, not only a rule for merchants.

column5: deeds weighed by YHWH
column6: Hannah calls YHWH a God of knowledge by whom deeds are weighed. This condenses the commentary's claim that conduct is assessed by a precise, nonpartial standard.

column5: false balances in grain trade
column6: Amos exposes merchants who shrink the measure, enlarge the shekel, and falsify balances. It gives the commentary's cheated measure a prophetic social setting in which such trade is itself judged.

column5: no human ransom can be given to God
column6: The commentary says no substitute payment is accepted on the final day; this psalm denies that a person can give God a ransom for a brother, making the limit of monetary exchange explicit.

column5: no ransom for a murderer
column6: The commentary notes retaliation may be turned to blood-money when the victim's kin forgive; Numbers forbids taking a ransom for a murderer liable to death. The contrast marks a concrete legal difference about substitution for bloodshed.

column5: ransom imposed for a life
column6: Where an owner is liable after his ox kills, Exodus allows a ransom imposed for his life. Read beside Numbers 35 and the commentary, it shows that biblical law distinguishes cases in which a life-payment can and cannot replace liability.

column5: exchange for one's life
column6: Jesus asks what a person could give in exchange for his life. It is a direct New Testament formulation of the commentary's final limit on offering an equivalent or ransom.

column5: the Son of Man's life as ransom
column6: The commentary invokes a day when no offered substitute can be accepted; Mark calls the Son of Man's life a ransom for many. The shared payment image leads to a specifically Christian resolution rather than a general commercial analogy.

column5: another person's debt charged to Paul
column6: Paul tells Philemon to charge any wrong or debt owed by Onesimus to Paul. This concrete assumption of another's obligation illuminates the commentary's language of putting one thing in another's place.

column5: unatoned blood and the land
column6: Numbers says bloodshed pollutes the land and is not expiated except by the shedder's blood. It gives a legal-theological form to the commentary's fear that spilled blood must not simply disappear without answer.

column5: God remembers blood and the afflicted cry
column6: The commentary speaks of blood lost if it is not avenged; the psalm says the seeker of blood remembers and does not forget the afflicted. Divine remembrance answers the image of vanished blood.

column5: martyrs ask when their blood will be avenged
column6: The slain cry to the sovereign Judge for judgment and vengeance of their blood on earth. Revelation preserves the commentary's unresolved-blood image inside an explicitly eschatological court appeal.

column5: vengeance, recompense, and a coming day
column6: “To me belong vengeance and recompense” is followed by the nearness of calamity. It closely joins the commentary's divine punitive anger, payment in return, and inevitable day.

column5: vengeance belongs to God who repays
column6: Paul prohibits private vengeance because God says, “I will repay.” This gives the commentary's account of divine wrath as punitive recompense a disciplined ethical implication.

column5: day of wrath, distress, ruin, darkness
column6: Zephaniah layers several “days” within the day of YHWH: wrath, distress, devastation, darkness. It is a close biblical realization of the commentary's severe day that bears many events within it.

column5: who can stand on the day of his coming
column6: Malachi asks who can endure and stand when the Lord appears. The verse binds the commentary's day, standing before the living Judge, and purgative punishment in one scene.

column5: wicked do not stand in judgment
column6: The psalm says the wicked will not stand in the judgment, supplying a precise biblical reverse of the commentary's picture of creatures standing before the Sustainer on the resurrection day.

column5: great day of wrath and ability to stand
column6: Revelation announces the great day of divine wrath and asks who can stand. It directly joins the commentary's two images of punitive anger and rising before the final authority.

column5: dead live and corpses rise
column6: Isaiah summons the dead to live and the corpses to rise. This is a direct resurrection counterpart to the commentary's qiyāmah, when creatures stand before God.

column5: Hebrew yequmun, “they shall rise”
column6: The commentary develops q-w-m from upright standing to resurrection; Isaiah's yequmun, “they shall rise,” uses the Hebrew cognate qûm in an actual resurrection proclamation, not merely a lexical resemblance.

column5: awakening from dust to life or disgrace
column6: Daniel's sleepers in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and some to abhorrence. It gives the commentary's standing resurrection a divided recompense.

column5: all stand before God's judgment seat
column6: Paul says all people will stand before the judgment seat of God. This provides the exact bodily-postural form of the commentary's creatures standing before the living, sustaining Judge.

column5: all appear to receive what is due
column6: All must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due for deeds done in the body. It combines the commentary's public standing, account, and equivalent return.

column5: God fixed a day to judge the world
column6: Paul announces a day fixed for judging the world in righteousness, guaranteed by resurrection. It is a direct day-of-judgment and resurrection formulation alongside Mālik yawm al-dīn.

column5: dead stand before throne; books and deeds judged
column6: The dead, great and small, stand before the throne; books are opened and they are judged by their deeds. This closely matches the commentary's standing, accounting, and exact recompense scene.

column5: time for wrath, judgment, and reward
column6: The verse announces God's wrath, the time to judge the dead, reward servants, and destroy destroyers. It gives a compact New Testament counterpart to punishment and payment on the decisive day.

column5: day of wrath and righteous judgment
column6: Paul speaks of storing up wrath for the day when God's righteous judgment is revealed. It directly supports the commentary's reading of divine wrath as judicial punishment rather than emotion alone.

column5: God repays each according to works
column6: The next verse defines that righteous judgment as repayment according to works. It supplies the commentary's payment-and-balance logic without needing a literal marketplace.

column5: account on the day of judgment
column6: Jesus says people will render account for every careless word on the day of judgment. The explicit account sharpens the commentary's dīn as reckoning, including what might otherwise be forgotten.

column5: God brings every hidden deed into judgment
column6: Ecclesiastes says God brings every deed, including hidden good or evil, into judgment. It supplies the commentary's claim that no person can be absent from or concealed in the account.

column5: no creature hidden; all exposed before God
column6: Hebrews says no creature is hidden and all are laid bare before the one to whom account is due. It is a close counterpart to the commentary's insistence that no one can evade the day.

column5: YHWH as judge, lawgiver, and king
column6: Isaiah names YHWH judge, lawgiver, and king in one confession. It makes concrete the commentary's definition of the sovereign as one who rules by command and prohibition.

column5: Ancient of Days seated on a throne
column6: Daniel's Ancient of Days takes his flaming throne before the court convenes. It supplies a royal judicial scene for the commentary's owner of the decisive day.

column5: Aramaic malku, everlasting kingdom
column6: The commentary's m-l-k identifies the day’s sovereign; Daniel's Aramaic malku, “kingdom,” shares that Semitic root and names an everlasting dominion granted in the court vision.

column5: Head of Days, throne, books, standing court
column6: 1 Enoch depicts the Head of Days seated on the throne of glory, books opened, and the heavenly court standing. It is an unusually close Second Temple expansion of the commentary's ruler, standing, and account scene.

column5: the earth and Sheol return their deposits
column6: At the resurrection the earth and Sheol give back what was entrusted to them. The return of what is owed gives the commentary's due-payment image a resurrection form.

column5: earth and dust give up the dead
column6: 4 Ezra says earth and dust surrender those asleep in them, and the storehouses surrender souls. It supplies a detailed Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to the commentary's resurrection day.

column5: the Most High appears on the judgment seat
column6: Immediately after the dead are returned, 4 Ezra places the Most High on the judgment seat. The sequence aligns resurrection with the sovereign's final adjudication.

column5: all pass before God; three books opened
column6: The rabbinic account of Rosh Hashanah has all creatures pass before God and speaks of heavenly books for verdicts. It interprets judgment and record imagery as an annually enacted reckoning.

column5: “Did you conduct business faithfully?”
column6: At heavenly judgment, faithful business dealing is named among the first questions asked. It directly carries the commentary's market-scale ethics into personal eschatological accountability.

column5: lend in need and repay on time
column6: Sirach instructs one to lend to a neighbor in need and repay the neighbor at the appointed time. It closely parallels the commentary's concrete debt with a fixed term before that debt becomes an image of judgment.

column5: severe judgment for rulers
column6: Wisdom warns that a severe judgment comes upon those in high places. It turns the commentary's kingly hierarchy back upon human rulers, who too face the sovereign Judge.

column5: forgiven sins and forgiven debtors
column6: Luke's prayer asks forgiveness of sins because the pray-ers forgive everyone indebted to them. It makes the commentary's proximity of debt and recompense into an explicit moral and devotional analogy.

column5: forgive debts as debtors are forgiven
column6: Matthew's prayer names moral forgiveness as the mutual release of debts. It gives a New Testament path by which commercial obligation is transposed into accountability before God.

column5: no release until the last lepton is paid
column6: Jesus' legal warning ends with payment of the last small coin before release. It provides the commentary's exact-price and due-debt image in a judicial setting.

column5: king returns and calls servants to account
column6: After receiving kingship, the returning ruler summons servants to learn what their trading has gained. Kingship, commercial calculation, and reckoning meet in one parable.

column5: Hebrew yaqum; witnesses establish a matter
column6: The commentary joins q-w-m, standing, and a witness who may forget. Deuteronomy's yaqum, from Hebrew qûm, says one witness cannot “rise” alone and requires corroborating testimony to establish a matter.

column5: reward and repayment according to work
column6: The returning Lord brings recompense to repay each according to work. It is a concise final-payment counterpart to the commentary's balance and day of return.

column5: coming judge repays each according to practice
column6: The verse following the question about an exchange for life says the Son of Man will come and repay each according to practice. It keeps ransom's limit and deed-for-deed recompense together.

column5: resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment
column6: Those in the tombs come out either to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment. It gives the commentary's standing resurrection its two-sided outcome.

column5: royal throne of final judgment
column6: The Son of Man comes in glory and sits on his glorious throne. This supplies a visibly royal form for the commentary's owner and ruler of the judgment day.

column5: eternal punishment and eternal life
column6: The final separation ends in eternal punishment for one group and eternal life for the other. It states the opposed outcomes implied by the commentary's recompense and divine wrath.

column5: God repays each according to work
column6: Job's speaker says God repays humans according to their work and lets each find what accords with their way. It gives the commentary's equivalent payment a direct wisdom formulation.

column5: God repays affliction to afflicters
column6: God is said to be just in repaying affliction to those who afflict believers. This is a specific final-judgment use of the commentary's reciprocal payment and punitive wrath.

column5: day of vengeance and year of recompense
column6: Isaiah names a day of YHWH's vengeance and a year of recompense. It explicitly pairs a decisive time with retaliation and payment.

column5: each person gives an account to God
column6: After saying all stand before God's judgment seat, Paul says each will give an account of self to God. This supplies the verbal accounting element distinct from the physical standing of verse 10.

column5: deeds follow and reward is displayed
column6: 4 Ezra says the work follows the person and the reward is displayed. It fills out the prior judgment-seat scene with the commentary's exact return for what was done.

column5: deeds preserved for many days
column6: Jeremiah orders the sealed and open deeds stored so they may last many days. It adds durable documentary memory to the commentary's concern that a witness can forget an obligation.

column5: sabbatical release of a loan
column6: The sabbatical law requires a creditor to release what was lent to a neighbor. It offers a Torah counterpoint to the commentary's debt coming due: a fixed time can cancel rather than exact an obligation.

column5: day of YHWH, wrath, sinners destroyed
column6: Isaiah calls the coming day cruel, full of wrath and fierce anger, to destroy sinners. It supplies another prophetic rendering of the commentary's day as a devastating event rather than a neutral unit of time.

column5: great and very terrible day
column6: Joel calls the day of YHWH great and exceedingly terrible and asks who can endure it. Its question of endurance complements the commentary's scene of people standing before the Judge.

column5: black horse carrying a balance
column6: Revelation's apocalyptic balance belongs to famine rationing and prices, not an impartial courtroom scale. That different use helps delimit the commentary's moralized, upright-balance image while retaining its economic force.

column5: measure used becomes measure received
column6: Jesus says the measure one uses will be measured back. It turns the commentary's exact measure into a reciprocal ethical rule, though it does not portray a literal final balance.

column5: steward commanded to render an account
column6: The steward must give an account of management before losing his position; the following scene concerns debtors and their bills. It supplies an administrative form of the commentary's account-and-debt imagery.

column5: Hillel's prosbul and sabbatical debts
column6: Hillel's prosbul responds to lenders withholding loans as the release year approaches, reworking Deuteronomy's debt law through a court procedure. It shows a rabbinic legal reading of how written obligation and mercy coexist.

column5: seven chronological questions for witnesses
column6: The Mishnah tests witnesses by sabbatical cycle, year, month, day, hour, and place. It offers a later Jewish legal answer to the commentary's concern that a witness may lose the event from memory.

column5: Matthean debt as sins before the heavenly King
column6: In his homily on Matthew 18:23–35, Chrysostom reads the enormous debt as sins forgiven by the heavenly King and the fellow servant's debt as an interpersonal claim. This interpretation makes the parable's monetary reckoning a moral account.

column5: Egypt given as Israel's ransom and exchange
column6: Isaiah pictures God giving Egypt, Cush, and Seba as Israel's ransom or exchange. Its historical divine substitution contrasts with the commentary's final-day claim that an offered equivalent cannot be accepted.
